Michele Malejki, Global Head of Social Impact at HP Inc. and Executive Director of the HP Foundation October 19, 2026 Key Takeaways HP's research shows workers are prioritizing transferable skills and adaptability in the age of AI. HP LIFE has reached more than 1 million learners so far in 2026, with strong demand for AI, business and professional skills training. HP’s research reveals 66% of Gen Z workers say access to upskilling opportunities makes them less anxious about AI’s impact on their role. For employers, the implication is clear: pair investment in AI with accessible learning opportunities that help people use it and adapt as work changes. The more workers use AI, the more they recognize that career resilience will depend on distinctly human skills. New findings from HP's Work Relationship Index suggest that greater AI fluency is not reducing the perceived need for adaptability, critical thinking, and continuous learning. Instead, workers with access to the most advanced AI tools are more focused on building the skills needed to navigate a future where roles, industries, and career paths continue to evolve. We're seeing that shift reflected in how people are choosing to learn. Across HP's skills programs, demand for both AI-focused training and human-centered skills continues to grow, reinforcing a clear message: in the age of AI, workforce readiness is about more than technology adoption. It's about helping people build the confidence and capabilities to evolve alongside it. Why are workers rethinking career success in the age of AI? Workers acknowledge that keeping pace with technology requires more than technical expertise. HP's research found that workers who use AI agents are more likely to believe their roles will become harder to define and more likely to worry about being replaced by AI or workers with AI expertise. The research also shows that workers place a high priority on skills that can help them adapt. Nearly six in ten workers now prioritize building transferable skills over climbing a traditional career ladder, and more than half believe career paths are becoming less linear in the AI era. Workers also recognize the importance of distinctly human capabilities. Nearly three-quarters say adaptability will be essential in the age of AI, while creative problem-solving and collaboration rank among the most important skills for future success. What are workers choosing to learn? One of the clearest indicators of workforce priorities is where people are investing their learning time. Learners are not choosing between technical and human skills. They are investing in both. HP LIFE , the HP Foundation's free business and digital skills program, has already reached more than one million learners globally in 2026, reaching that milestone earlier than in any previous year and pointing to accelerating demand for practical skills training. The most popular courses include AI for Beginners , AI for Business Professionals , and Data Science & Analytics . At the same time, learners are pursuing courses such as Critical Thinking in the AI Era and Professional Networking for Career Growth , reflecting interest in both AI knowledge and skills that apply across roles and career paths. How can access to learning help workers navigate AI? HP's Work Relationship Index suggests that access to learning can play an important role in helping workers navigate change with confidence. Among Gen Z workers, 66% say access to upskilling opportunities makes them less anxious about AI's impact on their role. For employers, this finding is a reason to consider access to learning alongside access to AI tools. Giving people opportunities to ask questions, experiment, and develop new skills should be part of how organizations introduce AI into work. Expanding access to skills and opportunity At HP, we believe the future of work should work for everyone. That means helping prepare the future workforce by expanding access to technology, digital skills, and economic opportunity as part of our goal to accelerate the future of work for 150 million people by 2030. HP’s social impact work is focused not only on expanding skills, but on reaching disconnected communities and people most vulnerable to economic shocks — those at greatest risk of being left behind as technology reshapes work. From supporting entrepreneurship and digital literacy through HP LIFE to expanding access to learning through partners such as Girl Rising and YMCA, HP and the HP Foundation are working to help more people build the confidence, opportunity, and future-ready capabilities needed to participate and thrive in a changing world. That commitment also comes to life through HP’s Future of Work Accelerator , which supports organizations helping young people and underserved communities access skills and career opportunities. As technology analyst Rob Enderle’s coverage of the Accelerator’s Pitch Fest highlights, practical experience and pathways into work are important complements to learning as AI reshapes the workplace. For business leaders, the next step is to make learning part of AI adoption: give people the opportunity to build AI fluency, strengthen critical thinking and collaboration, and practice applying those skills to their work. The career advantage will come from being able to use new tools and keep adapting as those tools, and the work itself, change. Footnotes and disclaimers About HP's Work Relationship Index In partnership with the National Research Group (NRG), HP conducted a survey of 19,506 desk-based workers across 15 countries from 7 April -13 May 2026. The countries included United States, Canada, Mexico, Brazil, UK, France, Germany, Spain, Italy, Saudi Arabia, India, Australia, Japan, Indonesia, and China.
